final_answer:
Bottom line: under the Guidelines, it should not matter which district is chosen, so long as ONE office brings ONE consolidated prosecution that reaches the conduct in both states. Neither office has a built-in sentencing advantage, and the doctor gains nothing by being split between two offices.

1. Guideline range is the same in either district. Section 1347 fraud is guided by USSG §2B1.1, and §2B1.1 is a §3D1.2(d) offense (loss-based, grouped). Under §1B1.3(a)(2), relevant conduct for such offenses includes all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction, whether charged or not. So even if the South Carolina office indicts only the South Carolina claims, the Georgia false claims (same practice, same type of scheme) can be counted as relevant conduct to aggregate loss, and the reverse is also true. The loss table, the federal health care offense enhancement in §2B1.1(b)(7) (government health care program loss thresholds), and other enhancements would therefore be driven by the combined loss either way. Charged-versus-uncharged status does not change the range, though uncharged conduct must be proven by a preponderance and the Commission's 2024 §1B1.3(c) only excludes conduct for which the defendant was charged and acquitted.

2. No circuit-law tilt that I could verify. The Fourth Circuit (D.S.C.) and Eleventh Circuit (S.D. Ga.) have both been described as treating the §2B1.1 loss rule, including intended loss, as applicable (the Third Circuit's Banks decision is the outlier). More importantly, Amendment 827 (eff. Nov. 1, 2024) moved the actual/intended loss definitions from commentary into the guideline text, largely mooting the Kisor/commentary-deference dispute. I did not find a materially different circuit rule on relevant conduct, grouping, or loss that would favor one district. I did not verify any Fourth/Eleventh Circuit split exhaustively.

3. Why consolidation matters. If both offices prosecute separately, the second sentencing court is directed by §5G1.3(b) to run the sentence concurrently with (and credit time on) the first sentence where the other offense is relevant conduct already taken into account. That is, separate prosecutions of the same relevant conduct are designed to approximate, not exceed, the total penalty from a single proceeding. Splitting the case therefore yields no extra time and risks the second court being bound to concurrency. A single indictment also avoids double-jeopardy/vindictiveness and coordination issues.

4. Which office, practically: the one with proper venue over the most counts. Venue is a constitutional/statutory limit (Art. III §2, Sixth Amendment, Fed. R. Crim. P. 18; 18 U.S.C. §3237(a) for continuing offenses and offenses using interstate commerce or mail). A district can only charge counts (each §1347 execution of the scheme, with a 10-year statutory maximum per count, 20 if serious bodily injury, life if death) whose conduct occurred in, or moved through, that district. Statutory maximums matter because the Guidelines range is capped by them, and §5G1.2(d) permits stacking consecutive terms only when the total punishment exceeds the statutory maximum of the highest count. So the best office is the one whose district can lawfully charge the broadest scheme (e.g., where the billing entity, claims submission, processing, or his main practice/payer connection sits), with the most counts and highest cumulative statutory maximum. On the facts given I cannot say whether that is D.S.C. or S.D. Ga.; if the claims were submitted from or routed through both states to a payer in one district, that district can indict everything. If each state's claims are only venue-proper in its own district, the offices should coordinate, one should take the lead on the combined loss as relevant conduct, and the other should hold off or dismiss to avoid the §5G1.3 concurrency effect.

Caveats: I could not retrieve primary text of every provision (relied on USSC and search summaries for several), and venue facts are unknown. Status is answered with the stated conditions.

authorities.title: Relevant Conduct
authorities.proposition: For offenses groupable under §3D1.2(d), relevant conduct includes same course of conduct/common scheme acts, charged or not; 2024 subsection (c) excludes charged-and-acquitted conduct

authorities.title: Imposition of sentence on defendant subject to undischarged term of imprisonment
authorities.proposition: Where undischarged term resulted from offense that is relevant conduct, sentence runs concurrently and is adjusted for time served

authorities.title: Offenses begun in one district and completed in another
authorities.proposition: Continuing offenses using mail/interstate commerce may be prosecuted in any district through which commerce moves (as described in search result summary)

authorities.proposition: Actual/intended loss definitions now in guideline text, mooting commentary-deference split

authorities.title: Health care fraud
authorities.proposition: Per-count statutory maximum 10 years (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death); stated from background knowledge, not fetched
